accepted_regressions: val5 tail: P99.9/L rose from 4.15 to 8.70 (+110%). The share of reads with errors above 5L rose from 0.023% (13 reads) to 1.40% (788 reads), and the tail metric from 3.25 to 5.38. This is accepted because val5's core error improved from 12.98% to 1.44%, its MAE/L from 0.571 to 0.366, and its share of reads above 1L from 19.5% to 11.3%.

val7 tail: P99.9/L rose from 6.07 to 6.79 (+12%). The share of reads with errors above 5L rose from 0.245% to 0.890% (1,061 to 3,878 reads), and the tail metric from 2.73 to 4.78. This is accepted because val7's core error improved from 55.43% to 9.35% and its MAE/L from 0.676 to 0.508.

val4 tail: P99.9/L rose from 3.66 to 5.36 (+46%), and the share of reads above 5L from 0.031% to 0.110% (261 to 921 reads). This is accepted because val4's core error improved from 34.67% to 0.07% and its MAE/L from 0.544 to 0.074.

val1 tail: P99.9/L rose from 4.02 to 5.59 (+39%), and reads above 5L from 21 to 73 (0.05% to 0.18%). This is accepted because val1's core error improved from 2.99% to 0.05% and its MAE/L from 0.449 to 0.145.
Training case whisper: P99.9/L rose from 2.15 to 2.81 (+31%), with no reads above 5L in either model. MAE/L improved from 0.571 to 0.038.

The model now overpredicts in extreme cases, which the fixed-latency incumbent never did. The largest overpredictions are about 10 to 14L (for example gap_sssp +1,538 cycles and val9 +910 cycles). They are rare: in val9, 315 of 2.07M reads have errors above 5L.
contract_findings: No demonstrated violation. Each read's prediction is computed once, in predict(), from model state and the current admission. It is returned as the column command time plus read_latency, or now + forward_latency for a read forwarded from a buffered write. Writes return now + 1. Returned values are never revised.

Inputs are within the interface. The model uses only the fields of Access (address, type, levels), the current cycle, and Hardware configuration (timings, level sizes, write capacity and watermarks). It uses no workload identity, fixed addresses, oracle completions or future requests. The Little's-law arrival estimate uses the model's own earlier predicted completion times.

Parameters: parameters.json is empty, and every parameter is declared through Parameters::number with a range that contains its default. rp_adjust = -1 is described as an empirically observed one-cycle offset between row-conflict and row-hit latency. It is a single global value, not specific to any workload.

Interpretive risk, not a demonstrated violation. The model contains substantial controller-like machinery: per-bank row windows with row-hit-first insertion, calendars of column and ACT commands, and a write buffer with watermark-driven write mode that picks which write to drain first (advance() and drain_one()). This comes close to the 'no internal command scheduler' clause. However, it runs only when a request is admitted, not every cycle. It books resources once to compute a prediction immediately and never holds back or re-times a prediction. I treat it as an approximate resource-reservation model rather than a demonstrated scheduler.

The source comments admit one known modeling gap: reads admitted before the write buffer crosses its high watermark are underpredicted when a forced drain follows. This is disclosed and consistent with the fixed-prediction design. It is a likely contributor to the remaining two-sided tails.
improvements: Training mean core error fell from 23.67% to 0.54% (-23.13 pp, -97.7%). All 14 training cases improved. Eleven are now below 0.4%, and the worst is lbm at 5.92% (was 67.19%).

Validation mean core error fell from 24.90% to 0.85% (-24.05 pp, -96.6%). All 14 validation cases improved. Twelve are now below 0.5%, including val3 (67.24% to 0.47%), val4 (34.67% to 0.07%) and val14 (33.90% to 0.14%).

Request MAE/L fell from 0.5425 to 0.1021 on training (-81.2%) and from 0.5309 to 0.0934 on validation (-82.4%). It improved in every case. Low-latency, low-contention cases are now nearly exact: kstar, maxclique, llama7b, val6, val12 and val13 are at or below 0.004 MAE/L.
The incumbent's systematic underprediction is essentially gone. Mean signed drift/L moved from -0.5425 to -0.0030 on training and from -0.5309 to -0.0042 on validation.

Tails improved on average. Mean P99.9/L fell from 4.38 to 3.27 on training (-25%) and from 3.49 to 3.14 on validation (-10%). The tail metric fell by 46% on training and 32% on validation. On training, reads with errors above 5L fell from 6,445 to 4,578, and no training case got worse on this count.

The share of reads with errors above 1L fell sharply almost everywhere. Examples: arizona from 20.4% to 3.9%, bravo from 17.0% to 0.44%, mcf from 32.2% to 0.02%, val2 from 11.0% to 0.39%, val14 from 17.3% to 1.6%.

Measurement coverage increased or stayed the same, so the candidate was compared on at least as many matched reads as the incumbent. Examples: val9 from 0.863 to 0.998, val10 from 0.918 to 0.998, val2 from 0.879 to 0.935, lbm from 0.973 to 0.994.
iteration:1:decision.rationale: No contract violation is demonstrated. Every mechanical integrity signal is clean: address_mismatch_pairs is 0 in all 28 cases, admission counts match the oracle, and parameters.json is empty, so the declared defaults apply. The model returns each read prediction once, at admission, as the column command time plus read_latency. It never revises a prediction. It uses only the current Access, the current cycle, Hardware configuration and its own earlier predictions. It does not use workload names, fixed addresses, oracle completions or future requests. The incumbent is the seed FixedLat model (now + read_latency), and the stage-entry reference is numerically identical to it, so both comparisons give the same result. The improvement is large and holds in every case. Training (14 single-core cases): mean core error fell from 23.67% to 0.54% (-23.13 pp, -97.7%), request MAE/L from 0.5425 to 0.1021 (-81.2%), signed drift/L from -0.5425 to -0.0030, P99.9/L from 4.38 to 3.27 (-25.2%) and the tail metric from 2.41 to 1.30 (-46%). Validation (14 anonymized single-core cases): mean core error fell from 24.90% to 0.85% (-24.05 pp, -96.6%), MAE/L from 0.5309 to 0.0934 (-82.4%), signed drift/L from -0.5309 to -0.0042, P99.9/L from 3.49 to 3.14 (-10.0%) and the tail metric from 2.02 to 1.36 (-32%). All 28 cases improve on both core error and MAE/L, including the worst ones: training case lbm went from 67.19% to 5.92%, and validation cases val3 from 67.24% to 0.47% and val7 from 55.43% to 9.35%. These gains are not artifacts of coverage. Candidate coverage is equal or higher in every case: for example val9 rose from 0.863 to 0.998, val10 from 0.918 to 0.998 and whisper from 0.952 to 0.998. The only decreases are val4 (-0.0001) and val5 (-0.00003), which are negligible. The gains are not cancellation either. Signed core error is close in size to absolute core error (training +0.37 vs 0.54; validation -0.84 vs 0.85), so the headline is not averaging opposite errors, and MAE/L is itself an absolute measure. The candidate does regress on some tails. The fixed-latency incumbent only ever underpredicted. The candidate errs in both directions, and on four validation cases its 5L-error frequency and P99.9 got worse. The largest case is val5, where the share of reads with errors above 5L rose from 0.023% to 1.40% and P99.9/L rose from 4.15 to 8.70. Across validation, reads with errors above 5L rose from 3,100 to 6,749, most of them in val7 (+2,817), val5 (+775) and val4 (+660). On training, the same count fell from 6,445 to 4,578, and no training case got worse. These tails are rare compared with a reduction in core error of about 24 pp and in MAE/L of about 82%. In each affected case the share of reads with errors above 1L also fell sharply (val7 from 31.0% to 20.6%, val5 from 19.5% to 11.4%, val4 from 6.8% to 2.5%). On balance the benefit is decisive, so the candidate should be promoted, and the remaining weaknesses should be recorded.

uncertainty: Two cases still have large errors: lbm (core +5.92%, MAE/L 0.639, 28% of reads with errors above 1L) and val7 (core -9.35%, MAE/L 0.508, 20.6% above 1L). Their request-level signed drift is near zero (-0.020 in both), so large per-request errors in both directions largely cancel. Their core errors point in opposite directions, which suggests that write handling and bandwidth pressure are not yet modeled robustly.

The tail regressions show up only on validation (val1, val4, val5, val7): reads with errors above 5L rose from 3,100 to 6,749. On training the same count fell. Training alone may therefore understate how often the model makes extreme errors in both directions on unseen workloads.

The candidate and incumbent are compared on slightly different matched sets, because stable-ID matching depends on each model's closed-loop timing. The candidate's coverage is higher in almost every case, so this does not favor the candidate. Reads without a stable ID (up to about 12% in val11, and about 9% in bravo, whiskey, val8 and val14) are unmeasured for both models.

Each case has a single deterministic run with no confidence intervals. The margins on core error and MAE/L are so large that this does not affect the decision, but the size of the small per-case tail changes is uncertain.

Multicore behavior is untested. This is the single-core stage, so only group 1 was assessed. Single-core accuracy is where the improvement is measured, and it should be rechecked as a baseline in later multicore rounds.

Whether the reservation-timeline design counts as an 'internal command scheduler' depends on how the contract is interpreted. This review judged it permissible because every prediction is made immediately and once, at admission.

uncertainty: The core-error gains are concentrated. Removing lbm from training and val5 and val7 from validation turns the core-error comparison into a small regression (training 0.128% to 0.142%; validation 0.096% to 0.126%). The broad, consistent evidence for the change is the MAE/L and tail improvement, not the mean core error.

The new arrival estimate makes the model predict lower latency for reads that start a burst while no other read is in flight. Most low-contention cases now lean slightly toward underpredicting core cycles. This bias is small (under 0.3% per case) but systematic, and it could grow if the model is later tuned in the same direction.

val7 is still a serious failure: -8.16% core error, MAE/L 0.381, and 15.8% of reads more than 1L off. lbm shows +1.36% core error while its requests are underpredicted on average (signed drift -0.033), which suggests closed-loop and write-drain effects are still not well modelled.

The estimator uses only 16 recent samples and a median. How it behaves when workloads change phase is untested, and in the coming multicore stage, interleaved streams from several cores will change the in-flight counts and gap distributions it relies on.

Each case is a single deterministic run with no confidence intervals. Differences of about 0.01 pp in core error, or a few reads in the 5L counts, cannot be distinguished from closed-loop noise. The val5/val7/val4 tail reductions and the 32% validation MAE/L drop are far larger than that noise.

The candidate and incumbent are compared on slightly different matched sets, because matching depends on each model's closed-loop timing. The differences are under 0.2% of reads and favour neither model in a way that affects the decision. Reads without a stable ID (up to about 12% in val11) are unmeasured for both.

arrival_model=1 was presumably chosen on training data. Validation gains in MAE/L (-32%) and tails (-77% of reads above 5L) are larger than on training (-7% and -3%), which argues against overfitting to training. Test performance is still unknown.

accepted_regressions: Small validation core-error regressions in 8 of 14 cases: val2 0.011% to 0.136% (+0.125 pp), val1 0.054% to 0.156% (+0.10 pp, sign flipped from over- to underprediction), val14 0.139% to 0.181% (+0.042 pp), val9 0.036% to 0.067% (+0.030 pp), val8 0.081% to 0.107% (+0.026 pp), val11 0.250% to 0.268% (+0.018 pp), val10 0.031% to 0.042% (+0.010 pp) and val12 0.00004% to 0.0046% (+0.005 pp). Together these add about 0.36 pp, against about 2.5 pp of gains in val5, val7 and val4. Excluding val5 and val7, the validation mean rises from 0.096% to 0.126%. This is accepted because every affected case stays below 0.27%, and every one of them has equal or better MAE/L. For example, val1's MAE/L fell 36% and its reads above 5L went from 73 to 9.

Training core-error regressions: charlie 0.373% to 0.590% (+0.22 pp, +58%), bravo 0.054% to 0.109% (+0.055 pp), gap_sssp 0.508% to 0.538% (+0.03 pp), and under 0.01 pp each for arizona, omnetpp and whiskey. Excluding lbm, the training mean rises from 0.128% to 0.142%. This is accepted because charlie's MAE/L still improves (0.239 to 0.225) and its reads above 1L fall by 7.8%, and bravo's MAE/L and tails also improve.

A small shift toward underprediction. Training mean absolute signed drift/L rose from 0.0099 to 0.0109, with charlie going from -0.021 to -0.028 and lbm from -0.020 to -0.033. In validation, val1 went from +0.007 to -0.013 and val4 from +0.006 to +0.013. Signed core error is now negative in 11 of 14 validation cases. Accepted because the magnitudes are about 1-3% of L, while the validation mean absolute drift improved from 0.0063 to 0.0045.

The largest single underpredictions grew slightly: val1 from -619 to -790 cycles and val4 from -844 to -941. These are single reads, and both cases lower their counts of reads above 5L (73 to 9 and 921 to 214).
gap_sssp has 16 more reads with errors above 5L (2,673 to 2,689, 0.71% versus 0.72%), and bravo has 7 more (89 to 96). Both are negligible next to the training-wide reduction.
contract_findings: No demonstrated violation. Each read is predicted once, in predict(), as the column command time plus read_latency, or as now + forward_latency when it matches a buffered write. Writes return now + write_ack, which defaults to 1 as in the incumbent. Returned values are never revised.

New behaviour with arrival_model=1: the model keeps ring buffers of the last 16 intervals between consecutive read admissions, bucketed by how many of its own predicted reads are in flight. For reads admitted with nothing else in flight, it also keeps the interval from that read's predicted completion to the next admission. These are used only to estimate when the next read will arrive. All inputs are past admissions or the model's own earlier predictions. No future requests, oracle completions or oracle internals are used.

Parameters: parameters.json sets only arrival_model=1, a declared parameter inside its range [0,2]. The new parameters write_ack (default 1, range [1,100000]) and drain_after_reads (default 0) are declared with in-range defaults and keep the incumbent's behaviour. The code behind arrival_model=2 and drain_after_reads=1 is present but not enabled.
No workload-specific logic. The code does not use workload names, fixed addresses, or evaluation identities. All hardware facts come from the Hardware configuration.

Same interpretive risk as in the previous review, with no new scheduler-like machinery added. Per-bank row windows, the column and ACT calendars, and the watermark-driven write-drain replay are the same as in the incumbent. They still run only at admission, to compute a fixed prediction, so I again treat the design as a resource-reservation model rather than an internal command scheduler.

Mechanical integrity checks are clean. address_mismatch_pairs is 0 in all 28 cases, the model has no admissions without a recorded latency, and admission counts track the oracle's within closed-loop noise.
improvements: Validation request MAE/L fell from 0.0934 to 0.0635 (-0.030, -31.9%), and no case got worse. The largest gains were in val5 (0.366 to 0.160, -56%), val1 (0.145 to 0.093, -36%), val4 (0.074 to 0.049, -34%), val9 (0.0033 to 0.0025, -26%), val7 (0.508 to 0.381, -25%) and val12 (-18%).

Training request MAE/L fell from 0.1021 to 0.0946 (-7.3%), improving in 12 of 14 cases. The largest gains were in whisper (0.0377 to 0.0313, -17%), lbm (0.639 to 0.559, -12.6%), charlie (0.239 to 0.225, -5.6%) and gap_bfs (-3.2%).
Mean core error fell from 0.542% to 0.229% on training (-0.31 pp, -57.7%) and from 0.854% to 0.700% on validation (-0.15 pp, -18.0%).

The worst individual cases improved. lbm went from +5.92% to +1.36% core error (-4.56 pp, -77%), with its share of reads above 1L falling from 28.0% to 23.6%. val5 went from -1.44% to -0.13% (-1.31 pp, -91%). val7, the dominant remaining failure, went from -9.35% to -8.16% (-1.20 pp, -12.8%), with reads above 1L falling from 20.6% to 15.8%.

Severe tails fell sharply on validation. Reads with errors above 5L fell from 6,749 to 1,567 (-77%), with no case worse. Mean P99.9/L fell from 3.14 to 2.31 (-26.5%) and the tail metric from 1.36 to 0.89 (-34.5%). This reverses the val1, val4, val5 and val7 tail regressions accepted in the previous promotion. For example, val5's P99.9/L fell from 8.70 to 4.21 and val4's from 5.36 to 2.37.

Moderate tails fell as well. Reads with errors above 1L fell from 130,740 to 94,912 on validation (-27%) and from 290,387 to 248,709 on training (-14%). Every validation case has an equal or lower count, and every training case except gap_sssp (+3 reads).

Extreme overpredictions shrank substantially. The largest overprediction fell from 1,193 to 614 cycles in val5, from 1,224 to 609 in val7, from 1,017 to 390 in val4, from 743 to 332 in val1, from 1,452 to 1,233 in bravo and from 1,405 to 1,130 in lbm.

The candidate beats the stage-entry FixedLat reference in all 28 cases. Training core error falls from 23.67% to 0.23% (-99%) and MAE/L from 0.5425 to 0.0946 (-83%). Validation core error falls from 24.90% to 0.70% (-97%) and MAE/L from 0.5309 to 0.0635 (-88%). Validation reads above 5L fall from 3,100 to 1,567, so the candidate no longer has more severe tails than the stage-entry reference; val5 is effectively tied at 16 reads versus 13.

Measurement coverage is effectively unchanged. The candidate matches more reads in val4 (+499) and val7 (+397), where the largest gains occur. The biggest loss is 44 reads in val2 and charlie, out of about 293k and 106k respectively. The gains are not due to measuring fewer reads.
promotion_review.rationale: No contract violation is demonstrated. The mechanical integrity signals are clean: address_mismatch_pairs is 0 in all 28 cases, the model records a latency for every admission, and admission counts match the oracle's apart from small closed-loop differences also seen with the incumbent. The only change from the incumbent that affects behaviour is the parameter override arrival_model=1, which is inside its declared range [0,2]. With it, a read admitted while no other read is in flight gets a next-arrival estimate. The estimate comes only from past admission gaps and from the model's own earlier predicted completion times. It is used only when history shows that the next read usually arrives before the lone read returns. It limits how long buffered writes may delay that read while it waits for tRCD. This is statistical estimation from past observations, not inspection of future requests. The new write_ack parameter defaults to the old constant (1), and the new drain_after_reads defaults to off, so neither changes behaviour. The candidate improves both headline objectives on both groups. Training (14 single-core cases): mean core error fell from 0.542% to 0.229% (-0.31 pp, -57.7%) and request MAE/L from 0.1021 to 0.0946 (-7.3%). Validation (14 anonymized cases): mean core error fell from 0.854% to 0.700% (-0.15 pp, -18.0%) and MAE/L from 0.0934 to 0.0635 (-31.9%). MAE/L improves or stays the same in every validation case and in 13 of 14 training cases; omnetpp is within 0.00003 of the incumbent. Tails improve strongly on validation. Mean P99.9/L fell from 3.14 to 2.31 (-26.5%) and the tail metric from 1.36 to 0.89 (-34.5%). Reads with errors above 5L fell from 6,749 to 1,567 (-77%), with no validation case worse. This reverses the tail regressions the previous reviewer accepted: val5 788 to 16, val7 3,878 to 389, val4 921 to 214, val1 73 to 9. On training, reads above 1L fell by 14.4% and reads above 5L from 4,578 to 4,456. The two largest failures named in the previous round both shrink: lbm from +5.92% to +1.36% core error, and val7 from -9.35% to -8.16%. val5 improves from -1.44% to -0.13%. These gains are not coverage artifacts. Matched-read counts are essentially equal, and they are higher for the candidate in val4 (+499) and val7 (+397), where the largest gains occur. They are not cancellation either: MAE/L is absolute, and the validation signed core error (-0.699%) is almost the same as its absolute value. There is a real cost. Core error is slightly worse in 8 of 14 validation cases and 6 of 14 training cases, and the candidate now underpredicts core cycles more often. Without val5 and val7, validation mean core error rises from 0.096% to 0.126% (+0.03 pp, about +30% relative). Without lbm, training rises from 0.128% to 0.142% (+0.014 pp). Every regressed case stays below 0.6% core error, and most of them improve on MAE/L and tails at the same time. Against the stage-entry FixedLat reference, all 28 cases improve. Training core error falls from 23.67% to 0.23% and validation from 24.90% to 0.70%. MAE/L falls by 82.6% on training and 88.0% on validation, and validation reads above 5L fall from 3,100 to 1,567. Taken together, gains of about 2.5 pp of summed per-case core error, a 32% cut in validation MAE/L and a 77% cut in severe validation tails clearly outweigh about 0.36 pp of summed small regressions. Promote.

uncertainty: The core-error gains are concentrated. Removing lbm from training and val5 and val7 from validation turns the core-error comparison into a small regression (training 0.128% to 0.142%; validation 0.096% to 0.126%). The broad, consistent evidence for the change is the MAE/L and tail improvement, not the mean core error.

The new arrival estimate makes the model predict lower latency for reads that start a burst while no other read is in flight. Most low-contention cases now lean slightly toward underpredicting core cycles. This bias is small (under 0.3% per case) but systematic, and it could grow if the model is later tuned in the same direction.

val7 is still a serious failure: -8.16% core error, MAE/L 0.381, and 15.8% of reads more than 1L off. lbm shows +1.36% core error while its requests are underpredicted on average (signed drift -0.033), which suggests closed-loop and write-drain effects are still not well modelled.

The estimator uses only 16 recent samples and a median. How it behaves when workloads change phase is untested, and in the coming multicore stage, interleaved streams from several cores will change the in-flight counts and gap distributions it relies on.

Each case is a single deterministic run with no confidence intervals. Differences of about 0.01 pp in core error, or a few reads in the 5L counts, cannot be distinguished from closed-loop noise. The val5/val7/val4 tail reductions and the 32% validation MAE/L drop are far larger than that noise.

The candidate and incumbent are compared on slightly different matched sets, because matching depends on each model's closed-loop timing. The differences are under 0.2% of reads and favour neither model in a way that affects the decision. Reads without a stable ID (up to about 12% in val11) are unmeasured for both.

arrival_model=1 was presumably chosen on training data. Validation gains in MAE/L (-32%) and tails (-77% of reads above 5L) are larger than on training (-7% and -3%), which argues against overfitting to training. Test performance is still unknown.

contract_findings: No demonstrated violation. Each read is still predicted once in predict(). The prediction is the booked column time plus read_latency, or now + forward_latency when the read matches a buffered write. Writes return now + write_ack. Returned values are never revised.

arrival_model=3 is new. For reads admitted while other reads are in flight, it keeps, per in-flight count, the last 16 gaps between admissions and the last 16 intervals from the earliest predicted completion in flight to the next admission. It then chooses between two estimates of when the next read arrives: the burst continuing, or the burst ending after the oldest outstanding miss returns. All inputs are past admissions or the model's own earlier predictions. No future requests, oracle completions or oracle internals are used.

drain_after_reads=2 starts a forced write drain after the ACT of the latest booked read, rather than overlapping it. drain_block=1 makes reads admitted before the end of a drain the model has already booked wait for that end. Both change only how the model places its own reservations at admission. Neither adds per-cycle command selection, and neither holds back or re-times an issued prediction.

Parameters: parameters.json sets arrival_model=3 (range [0,3]), arrival_buckets=32 (range [1,65]), drain_after_reads=2 (range [0,2]) and drain_block=1 (range [0,2]), all within their declared ranges. col_slip defaults to 0, so its code path (slip_after) returns immediately. The defaults of the new parameters reproduce the incumbent's behaviour.
No workload-specific logic. The code does not use workload names, fixed addresses or evaluation identities. All hardware facts come from the Hardware configuration.

Interpretive risk, not a violation, same as in the earlier reviews. The reservation timeline, with per-bank row windows, column and ACT calendars and a watermark-driven replay of write drains, resembles controller logic. The new drain-placement options add to that resemblance. Everything still runs only at admission to compute a fixed prediction, so I treat it as a resource-reservation model.

iteration:3:decision.rationale:
No contract violation is demonstrated. The mechanical integrity checks are clean in all 28 cases: address_mismatch_pairs is 0, the model records a latency for every admission, and matched-read counts are within 0.02% of the incumbent's. The largest differences are val4 (-97 of about 839k reads) and val7 (+95 of about 436k). The source changes only add behaviour that the parameters must enable. With the frozen settings, that is arrival_model=3 with arrival_buckets=32, drain_after_reads=2 and drain_block=1, all inside their declared ranges; col_slip stays off. arrival_model=3 estimates when the next read will arrive. It uses only the model's past admission gaps and its own earlier predicted completion times: the gap from the earliest predicted completion in flight to the next admission, bucketed by how many reads are in flight. The two drain options only change where the model's own write drain is placed relative to reads it has already booked. Predictions are still made once, at admission, and never revised.

On the primary objectives, three of four headline measures improve and one is slightly worse. Training mean core error fell from 0.2293% to 0.2182% (-0.011 pp, -4.9%), or from 0.142% to 0.130% (-8.5%) without lbm. Training request MAE/L fell from 0.0946 to 0.0908 (-4.0%). Validation MAE/L fell from 0.0635 to 0.0601 (-5.4%). Validation mean core error rose from 0.6996% to 0.7092% (+0.0096 pp, +1.4%), and without val7 from 0.126% to 0.143% (+13%). Almost all of that comes from val4.

The MAE/L gain is modest but consistent. Among the cases whose metrics changed, MAE/L improved in 8 validation cases and worsened in 1 (val8, +0.9%). On training it improved in 8 and worsened in 2 (arizona +1.3%, gap_bfs +0.3%). The validation gain is larger than the training gain, which argues against overfitting to training. Summed per-case core-error changes nearly cancel across the two groups (-0.157 pp on training, +0.135 pp on validation), so core accuracy is essentially neutral overall. Signed bias shrinks: mean |signed drift|/L fell from 0.0109 to 0.0084 (-23.5%) on training and from 0.0045 to 0.0041 (-8.7%) on validation.

Moderate tails improve. Reads with errors above 1L fell from 248,709 to 238,627 (-4.1%) on training and from 94,912 to 87,701 (-7.6%) on validation. Validation mean P99.9/L fell from 2.31 to 2.24 (-2.9%) and the validation tail metric from 0.893 to 0.840 (-5.9%). Severe tails are mixed and small: reads above 5L fell from 4,456 to 4,352 (-2.3%) on training but rose from 1,567 to 1,609 (+2.7%) on validation, and training P99.9/L is +0.7%.

The gains are not due to lower coverage, and MAE/L is an absolute measure, so they are not cancellation. Against the stage-entry FixedLat reference the candidate keeps its very large advantage. Core error is 0.218% vs 23.67% on training and 0.709% vs 24.90% on validation. MAE/L is 0.0908 vs 0.5425 on training and 0.0601 vs 0.5309 on validation. Reads above 5L are 4,352 vs 6,445 on training and 1,609 vs 3,100 on validation.

This is the single-core stage, so no multicore trade-off applies. The improvement is incremental, not decisive. Still, a consistent 4-5% MAE/L reduction on both groups, lower bias and fewer moderate tails outweigh a roughly neutral core-error change whose main cost is one validation case that stays below 0.3%. Promote.

promotion_review.rationale:
No contract violation is demonstrated. The mechanical integrity checks are clean in all 28 cases: address_mismatch_pairs is 0, the model records a latency for every admission, and matched-read counts are within 0.02% of the incumbent's. The largest differences are val4 (-97 of about 839k reads) and val7 (+95 of about 436k). The source changes only add behaviour that the parameters must enable. With the frozen settings, that is arrival_model=3 with arrival_buckets=32, drain_after_reads=2 and drain_block=1, all inside their declared ranges; col_slip stays off. arrival_model=3 estimates when the next read will arrive. It uses only the model's past admission gaps and its own earlier predicted completion times: the gap from the earliest predicted completion in flight to the next admission, bucketed by how many reads are in flight. The two drain options only change where the model's own write drain is placed relative to reads it has already booked. Predictions are still made once, at admission, and never revised.

On the primary objectives, three of four headline measures improve and one is slightly worse. Training mean core error fell from 0.2293% to 0.2182% (-0.011 pp, -4.9%), or from 0.142% to 0.130% (-8.5%) without lbm. Training request MAE/L fell from 0.0946 to 0.0908 (-4.0%). Validation MAE/L fell from 0.0635 to 0.0601 (-5.4%). Validation mean core error rose from 0.6996% to 0.7092% (+0.0096 pp, +1.4%), and without val7 from 0.126% to 0.143% (+13%). Almost all of that comes from val4.

The MAE/L gain is modest but consistent. Among the cases whose metrics changed, MAE/L improved in 8 validation cases and worsened in 1 (val8, +0.9%). On training it improved in 8 and worsened in 2 (arizona +1.3%, gap_bfs +0.3%). The validation gain is larger than the training gain, which argues against overfitting to training. Summed per-case core-error changes nearly cancel across the two groups (-0.157 pp on training, +0.135 pp on validation), so core accuracy is essentially neutral overall. Signed bias shrinks: mean |signed drift|/L fell from 0.0109 to 0.0084 (-23.5%) on training and from 0.0045 to 0.0041 (-8.7%) on validation.

Moderate tails improve. Reads with errors above 1L fell from 248,709 to 238,627 (-4.1%) on training and from 94,912 to 87,701 (-7.6%) on validation. Validation mean P99.9/L fell from 2.31 to 2.24 (-2.9%) and the validation tail metric from 0.893 to 0.840 (-5.9%). Severe tails are mixed and small: reads above 5L fell from 4,456 to 4,352 (-2.3%) on training but rose from 1,567 to 1,609 (+2.7%) on validation, and training P99.9/L is +0.7%.

The gains are not due to lower coverage, and MAE/L is an absolute measure, so they are not cancellation. Against the stage-entry FixedLat reference the candidate keeps its very large advantage. Core error is 0.218% vs 23.67% on training and 0.709% vs 24.90% on validation. MAE/L is 0.0908 vs 0.5425 on training and 0.0601 vs 0.5309 on validation. Reads above 5L are 4,352 vs 6,445 on training and 1,609 vs 3,100 on validation.

This is the single-core stage, so no multicore trade-off applies. The improvement is incremental, not decisive. Still, a consistent 4-5% MAE/L reduction on both groups, lower bias and fewer moderate tails outweigh a roughly neutral core-error change whose main cost is one validation case that stays below 0.3%. Promote.

contract_findings: No demonstrated violation. The only difference from the incumbent is a new parameter, same_cycle_writes, declared through Parameters::number with default 0 and range [0,1]. Its default reproduces the incumbent exactly. parameters.json sets it to 1 and leaves arrival_model=3, arrival_buckets=32, drain_after_reads=2 and drain_block=1 as in the incumbent.

The parameter changes only the commit cutoff in advance(), from `until = now` to `until = now + 1`. Write commands that the model's own replay schedules at the admission cycle are committed before the read. Only writes admitted before `now` can be committed: a write admitted at `now` has earliest = now+1, and the current write is pushed after advance(). No future requests, oracle completions or oracle internals are used.

Each read is still predicted once in predict(), as the booked column time plus read_latency, or now + forward_latency when it matches a buffered write. Writes return now + write_ack. Returned values are never revised.
The physical rationale is generic. It assumes the controller chooses its command for cycle t before it sees a read admitted at t. Nothing depends on a workload, address or evaluation identity.

Mechanical integrity checks are clean in all 28 cases. address_mismatch_pairs is 0, and the model has zero admissions without a recorded latency. Admission counts track the oracle with the same small closed-loop offsets as the incumbent (for example bravo 1,136,693 vs 1,136,718).

Interpretive risk remains as in the previous reviews, with nothing new added. The reservation timeline with a watermark-driven replay of write drains resembles controller logic, but it runs only at admission to compute a fixed prediction.

No contract violation is demonstrated. The mechanical integrity checks are clean in all 28 cases. address_mismatch_pairs is 0, the model records a latency for every admission, and admission counts match the incumbent's small closed-loop offsets. The candidate differs from the incumbent in one way only: a new parameter, same_cycle_writes, declared with range [0,1] and default 0, which parameters.json sets to 1. The other four parameters are unchanged. The parameter affects only the commit cutoff in advance(). Write commands that the model's own replay schedules at the read's admission cycle are now committed before the read (until = now+1 instead of now). The read then pays that write's turnaround, and it is no longer forwarded from a write that has already left the buffer. The only writes that can be committed are ones admitted before `now`. Writes admitted at `now` have earliest = now+1, and the current write is pushed after advance(). No future or oracle information is used, and predictions are still made once and never revised.

The primary objectives improve in both groups. Training mean core error fell from 0.2182% to 0.1685% (-0.050 pp, -22.8%). Without lbm it fell from 0.130% to 0.0725% (-44%). Validation mean core error fell from 0.7092% to 0.4504% (-0.259 pp, -36.5%). The validation gain is not only val7: without val7 it fell from 0.143% to 0.096% (-33%). On validation, core error improved in 10 cases, worsened in 1 (val5, +0.027 pp) and was unchanged in 3. The dominant failure, val7, went from -8.08% to -5.06% (-3.02 pp, -37%), with MAE/L -4.2% and reads above 1L -6.5%. Request MAE/L fell 1.9% on training (0.09080 to 0.08909) and 4.2% on validation (0.06010 to 0.05758). MAE/L improved in 10 validation cases and worsened in 2; the worse ones are val13, +0.00006 absolute, and val3, +0.2%. On training it improved in 8 cases and worsened in 4, each by at most 0.16%.

The mechanism is visible in the request data. A recurring class of about -179-cycle extreme underpredictions disappeared: val10 -179 to -47, val13 -179 to -23, maxclique -179 to -12. These are consistent with reads that used to be forwarded from writes already issued. Moderate tails fell. Reads with errors above 1L fell from 87,701 to 81,162 (-7.5%) on validation, with no case worse, and from 238,627 to 234,539 on training. Without lbm, training fell from 29,984 to 25,657 (-14.4%). The validation tail metric fell from 0.840 to 0.758 (-9.7%) and the training tail metric from 1.259 to 1.222 (-2.9%).

The systematic underprediction flagged in the last two reviews is reduced. Signed core error without lbm moved from -0.080% to +0.028% on training. Without val7 it moved from -0.129% to -0.056% on validation. Validation cases with negative signed core error fell from 12 to 8. Validation regressions accepted last round are partly reversed: val4 0.285% to 0.234%, val1 0.183% to 0.170%, val2 0.162% to 0.014%.

There are costs. Severe tails did not improve: reads with errors above 5L rose from 4,352 to 4,512 (+3.7%) on training and from 1,609 to 1,628 (+1.2%) on validation. P99.9/L rose 0.25% on training and 1.0% on validation. gap_bfs core error doubled, from 0.10% to 0.21%. lbm, the worst training case, rose from 1.365% to 1.417%. These gains are not a coverage effect: matched reads are equal or slightly higher, for example val7 +140, val4 +132 and val2 +115. MAE/L is an absolute measure, so they are not cancellation either. Against the stage-entry FixedLat reference, core error is 0.169% vs 23.67% on training and 0.450% vs 24.90% on validation. MAE/L is 0.0891 vs 0.5425 on training and 0.0576 vs 0.5309 on validation. Reads above 5L are 4,512 vs 6,445 on training and 1,628 vs 3,100 on validation. This is the single-core stage, so there is no multicore trade-off. Core-error gains of 23-37%, consistent MAE/L gains, fewer moderate tails and smaller bias outweigh small increases in severe tails and a few small per-case regressions. Promote.

uncertainty: Each case is one deterministic closed-loop run with no confidence intervals. Differences of about 0.01 pp in core error, or tens of reads in the 5L counts, may be closed-loop perturbation. The val7 (-3.0 pp), val11, val2, gap_sssp and charlie gains are well above that level.

val7 is still the dominant failure at -5.06% core error, with MAE/L 0.351 and 14% of reads more than 1L off. Its mean request error is now positive (+0.019L) while core cycles are still underpredicted. So part of its core gain may come from higher predicted latency in general rather than from the critical-path mechanism being fixed, although its MAE/L and reads above 1L also fell.

Severe errors of ±1,000-2,300 cycles are not addressed. gap_sssp's share of absolute error above 5L rose from 0.52 to 0.60, and arizona, charlie and gap_bfs gained 5L reads. Rare, large two-sided errors remain the main unresolved weakness.

lbm (+1.42%) and val3 (-0.47%) are persistent failures that this change leaves unchanged or slightly worse. The training signed core mean is now positive (+0.127%), so further tuning in this direction could produce systematic overprediction.

This round tests a single parameter change, so the effect can be attributed cleanly. However, the within-cycle ordering it assumes has been validated only through end-to-end ChampSim metrics, not a separate causal test.
Multicore behaviour is untested. This is the single-core stage, and single-core accuracy should be rechecked as the baseline in later multicore rounds.

Reads without a stable ID are unmeasured for both models (about 9-12% in bravo, whiskey, val8, val11 and val14). The matched sets are nearly identical, slightly larger for the candidate, so coverage favours neither model.

contract_findings: No demonstrated violation. The only difference from the incumbent is a new parameter, same_cycle_writes, declared through Parameters::number with default 0 and range [0,1]. Its default reproduces the incumbent exactly. parameters.json sets it to 1 and leaves arrival_model=3, arrival_buckets=32, drain_after_reads=2 and drain_block=1 as in the incumbent.

The parameter changes only the commit cutoff in advance(), from `until = now` to `until = now + 1`. Write commands that the model's own replay schedules at the admission cycle are committed before the read. Only writes admitted before `now` can be committed: a write admitted at `now` has earliest = now+1, and the current write is pushed after advance(). No future requests, oracle completions or oracle internals are used.

Each read is still predicted once in predict(), as the booked column time plus read_latency, or now + forward_latency when it matches a buffered write. Writes return now + write_ack. Returned values are never revised.
The physical rationale is generic. It assumes the controller chooses its command for cycle t before it sees a read admitted at t. Nothing depends on a workload, address or evaluation identity.

Mechanical integrity checks are clean in all 28 cases. address_mismatch_pairs is 0, and the model has zero admissions without a recorded latency. Admission counts track the oracle with the same small closed-loop offsets as the incumbent (for example bravo 1,136,693 vs 1,136,718).

Interpretive risk remains as in the previous reviews, with nothing new added. The reservation timeline with a watermark-driven replay of write drains resembles controller logic, but it runs only at admission to compute a fixed prediction.
improvements: Validation mean core error fell from 0.7092% to 0.4504% (-0.259 pp, -36.5%). Without val7 it fell from 0.1426% to 0.0959% (-0.047 pp, -32.8%). 10 of 14 cases improved, 1 worsened and 3 were unchanged. The largest gains: val7 -8.076% to -5.059% (-3.02 pp), val11 0.263% to 0.009% (-0.254 pp), val2 0.162% to 0.014% (-0.148 pp), val14 0.174% to 0.059% (-0.116 pp), val4 0.285% to 0.234% (-0.051 pp), val8 0.110% to 0.064% (-0.046 pp).

Training mean core error fell from 0.2182% to 0.1685% (-0.050 pp, -22.8%). Without lbm it fell from 0.130% to 0.0725% (-44%). The largest gains: gap_sssp 0.485% to 0.065% (-0.42 pp, -87%), charlie 0.515% to 0.187% (-0.33 pp, -64%), bravo 0.123% to 0.032% (-0.09 pp), arizona 0.089% to 0.051%. Summed per-case gains are 0.88 pp, against 0.19 pp of summed regressions.

Validation request MAE/L fell from 0.06010 to 0.05758 (-4.2%): val11 -14.1%, val2 -12.5%, val8 -8.1%, val7 -4.2%, val14 -3.0%, val1 -2.2%, val4 -2.0%. Training MAE/L fell from 0.09080 to 0.08909 (-1.9%): gap_sssp -11.1%, omnetpp -11.4%, whiskey -10.3%, mcf -14%, gap_bfs -3.0%, charlie -2.1%. Every training case that got worse did so by at most 0.16%.

The underprediction bias shrank. Signed core error without lbm went from -0.080% to +0.028% on training, and without val7 from -0.129% to -0.056% on validation. Validation cases underpredicting core cycles fell from 12 to 8. Training mean |signed drift|/L fell from 0.00836 to 0.00746 (-10.8%): gap_sssp -0.0143 to -0.0074, charlie -0.0221 to -0.0139. On validation, excluding val7, it fell from 0.00418 to 0.00318 (-24%).

Moderate tails fell. Validation reads with errors above 1L fell from 87,701 to 81,162 (-7.5%), with no case worse: val7 -4,275, val11 -32%, val2 -27%, val8 -21%, val14 -8.9%. On training they fell from 238,627 to 234,539; without lbm from 29,984 to 25,657 (-14.4%), including gap_sssp -34.9%, omnetpp -22.8% and whiskey -21.8%. The validation tail metric fell 9.7% and the training tail metric 2.9%. P99 fell in val11 (158 to 99 cycles), val8 (113 to 79), val2 (66 to 57) and whiskey (93 to 68).

A class of recurring extreme underpredictions was removed. The worst underpredictions in val10, val13 and maxclique were each -179 cycles and became -47, -23 and -12. mcf went from -185 to -157, with its reads above 1L falling from 57 to 28. This matches the mechanism: reads are no longer forwarded from a write that has already issued.
Validation regressions accepted in the previous round are partly reversed: val4 0.285% to 0.234%, val1 0.183% to 0.170%, val2 0.162% to 0.014%, and val8 has 6 fewer reads above 5L.

The large advantage over the stage-entry FixedLat reference is kept and extended. Training core error is 0.169% vs 23.67% (-99.3%) and MAE/L 0.0891 vs 0.5425 (-83.6%). Validation core error is 0.450% vs 24.90% (-98.2%) and MAE/L 0.0576 vs 0.5309 (-89.2%). Reads above 5L are 4,512 vs 6,445 on training and 1,628 vs 3,100 on validation.
promotion_review.rationale:
No contract violation is demonstrated. The mechanical integrity checks are clean in all 28 cases. address_mismatch_pairs is 0, the model records a latency for every admission, and admission counts match the incumbent's small closed-loop offsets. The candidate differs from the incumbent in one way only: a new parameter, same_cycle_writes, declared with range [0,1] and default 0, which parameters.json sets to 1. The other four parameters are unchanged. The parameter affects only the commit cutoff in advance(). Write commands that the model's own replay schedules at the read's admission cycle are now committed before the read (until = now+1 instead of now). The read then pays that write's turnaround, and it is no longer forwarded from a write that has already left the buffer. The only writes that can be committed are ones admitted before `now`. Writes admitted at `now` have earliest = now+1, and the current write is pushed after advance(). No future or oracle information is used, and predictions are still made once and never revised.

The primary objectives improve in both groups. Training mean core error fell from 0.2182% to 0.1685% (-0.050 pp, -22.8%). Without lbm it fell from 0.130% to 0.0725% (-44%). Validation mean core error fell from 0.7092% to 0.4504% (-0.259 pp, -36.5%). The validation gain is not only val7: without val7 it fell from 0.143% to 0.096% (-33%). On validation, core error improved in 10 cases, worsened in 1 (val5, +0.027 pp) and was unchanged in 3. The dominant failure, val7, went from -8.08% to -5.06% (-3.02 pp, -37%), with MAE/L -4.2% and reads above 1L -6.5%. Request MAE/L fell 1.9% on training (0.09080 to 0.08909) and 4.2% on validation (0.06010 to 0.05758). MAE/L improved in 10 validation cases and worsened in 2; the worse ones are val13, +0.00006 absolute, and val3, +0.2%. On training it improved in 8 cases and worsened in 4, each by at most 0.16%.

The mechanism is visible in the request data. A recurring class of about -179-cycle extreme underpredictions disappeared: val10 -179 to -47, val13 -179 to -23, maxclique -179 to -12. These are consistent with reads that used to be forwarded from writes already issued. Moderate tails fell. Reads with errors above 1L fell from 87,701 to 81,162 (-7.5%) on validation, with no case worse, and from 238,627 to 234,539 on training. Without lbm, training fell from 29,984 to 25,657 (-14.4%). The validation tail metric fell from 0.840 to 0.758 (-9.7%) and the training tail metric from 1.259 to 1.222 (-2.9%).

The systematic underprediction flagged in the last two reviews is reduced. Signed core error without lbm moved from -0.080% to +0.028% on training. Without val7 it moved from -0.129% to -0.056% on validation. Validation cases with negative signed core error fell from 12 to 8. Validation regressions accepted last round are partly reversed: val4 0.285% to 0.234%, val1 0.183% to 0.170%, val2 0.162% to 0.014%.

There are costs. Severe tails did not improve: reads with errors above 5L rose from 4,352 to 4,512 (+3.7%) on training and from 1,609 to 1,628 (+1.2%) on validation. P99.9/L rose 0.25% on training and 1.0% on validation. gap_bfs core error doubled, from 0.10% to 0.21%. lbm, the worst training case, rose from 1.365% to 1.417%. These gains are not a coverage effect: matched reads are equal or slightly higher, for example val7 +140, val4 +132 and val2 +115. MAE/L is an absolute measure, so they are not cancellation either. Against the stage-entry FixedLat reference, core error is 0.169% vs 23.67% on training and 0.450% vs 24.90% on validation. MAE/L is 0.0891 vs 0.5425 on training and 0.0576 vs 0.5309 on validation. Reads above 5L are 4,512 vs 6,445 on training and 1,628 vs 3,100 on validation. This is the single-core stage, so there is no multicore trade-off. Core-error gains of 23-37%, consistent MAE/L gains, fewer moderate tails and smaller bias outweigh small increases in severe tails and a few small per-case regressions. Promote.

contract_findings: No demonstrated contract violation. The new mechanism counts reads the model itself booked that left the read queue before the current drain began and had not completed by the admission time. It uses the model's own issued predictions, stored in `outstanding` as {leave, done}. It then scales that count by a 256-admission EWMA of the observed write fraction, and optionally caps it with a limit derived from the Hardware config: (tRCD + read_latency + tCCDS - 1) / tCCDS.

Prediction still happens once, at admission. Reads return b.column + read_latency, or now + forward_latency for forwarded reads. Writes return now + write_ack. No issued prediction is revised afterwards. The expected-writeback count only changes internal booking state: how long the drain loop in predict() runs and when advance() leaves a forced drain.

I found no use of future requests, oracle internals, workload names, addresses or evaluation identities. Address comparisons are limited to forwarding from buffered writes, which the incumbent also does. The new parameters drain_pending=1 and pending_cap=1 are inside their declared ranges, and the defaults of 0 reproduce the incumbent's behaviour.

Mechanical integrity: address_mismatch_pairs is 0 in all 28 cases, no admission lacks a recorded latency, and changes in matched reads are negligible (-13 to +46 per case). The results are not affected by lost coverage.

An interpretive risk carried over from earlier reviews remains. The reservation timeline, with its write-mode replay and forced-drain logic, resembles controller machinery. It still runs only at admission, and I did not find a separate per-cycle command scheduler, so this is not a demonstrated violation.
improvements: Training core error falls from 0.1685% to 0.1014% (-0.067 pp, -39.8% relative), driven by lbm dropping from 1.417% to 0.463% (-0.954 pp, -67%). Noted but not enough to promote: lbm's MAE/L and tail frequency both get worse.

Training mean |signed drift|/L falls from 0.00746 to 0.00668 (-10.5%), and mean signed core error falls from +0.127% to +0.059%. lbm's signed drift/L falls from +0.0131 to +0.0047. This matches the modelled physics: reads that were outstanding before a drain began generate writebacks that keep the controller in write mode longer.

Small gains in other training cases: arizona core error falls from 0.0506% to 0.0311% (-0.0195 pp), gap_bfs MAE/L falls 1.9% and its reads above 1L fall 4.2%, and training reads above 1L excluding lbm fall 2.7%.

Small validation gains: val9 MAE/L falls 5.0%, val11 P99.9/L falls from 4.80 to 4.39 (-8.6%), and validation reads above 1L fall from 81,162 to 81,041 (-0.15%). None of these changes the validation core error by more than 0.0011 pp.

Coverage therefore does not explain any of the differences. The candidate's one headline gain is training core error, which falls from 0.1685% to 0.1014% (-0.067 pp, -39.8% relative). Almost all of that comes from one case: lbm drops from 1.417% to 0.463% (-0.954 pp, -67%). The per-request accuracy on lbm gets worse, though: MAE/L rises from 0.5168 to 0.5264 (+1.85%), reads above 1L rise from 208,882 to 210,914, P99.9/L rises from 3.19 to 3.30, and the worst errors grow at both ends (max +1,147 to +1,275 cycles, min -1,826 to -1,974 cycles). So the lbm gain comes from a better-balanced aggregate bias, not better latency prediction. Without lbm, training core error slightly worsens, from 0.0725% to 0.0736% (+0.001 pp, +1.4%). The other primary objective, request MAE/L, gets worse on training: 0.08909 to 0.09043 (+1.5%), with 5 of the 7 changed cases worse. Severe tails grow on training: reads above 5L go from 4,512 to 5,163 (+651, +14.4%), concentrated in charlie (+45%), gap_sssp (+9%) and arizona (+23%). Training P99.9/L rises 3.0%. Validation shows no benefit on any headline measure. Core error is unchanged (0.450407% vs 0.450424%), MAE/L rises 0.06%, P99.9/L rises 1.2% (val8 alone rises 18%), and reads above 5L go from 1,628 to 1,653. The dominant validation failure, val7 at -5.06% core error, is unchanged. Against the stage-entry FixedLat baseline, the candidate is still much better (training 0.101% vs 23.67% core error and 0.090 vs 0.543 MAE/L; validation 0.450% vs 24.90% and 0.058 vs 0.531). The incumbent holds the same advantage, so this comparison does not favour either. The gain is a bias correction in one training case. It did not carry over to validation and comes with worse MAE/L and more frequent severe tails, so it is not convincing enough to replace the incumbent.

iteration:6:decision.rationale:
No contract violation was demonstrated. The integrity checks are clean: address_mismatch_pairs is 0 in all 28 cases, and no model admission lacks a recorded latency. Oracle-side unpaired admissions are identical to the incumbent's, and matched-read counts change by at most ±0.15% in any case (largest: arizona −122 reads; val4 +363). The fix does not come from lower coverage.

I compared the incumbent source directly. Three behaviours change together: (1) col_slip, which already existed but was off, is turned on; (2) slip_sync is new, and a slipped read now also raises its bank's col_ok/pre_ok and, for row hits, read_horizon; (3) drain_after_reads=3 is new, so a forced drain now waits only for booked read ACTs. All three are general bandwidth and bank-timing rules tied to DDR timings. None depends on workload names, fixed addresses or future requests. Returned predictions are still computed once at admission and never revised; only internal calendar and bank state is updated.

Training (14 cases):
- Core error drops from 0.1685% to 0.1164% (−0.052 pp, −30.9%).
- Request MAE/L drops from 0.08909 to 0.08630 (−3.1%), and mean absolute drift/L from 0.00746 to 0.00436 (−41.6%).
- P99.9/L drops 1.6%. Reads with error above 5L fall from 4,512 to 4,191 (−7.1%); reads above 1L fall 3.6%.
- lbm, the worst training case, supplies about 96% of the core gain: 1.417% to 0.718% (−0.70 pp, −49%).
- Unlike the rejected round 5, lbm's request metrics also improve: MAE/L −2.3%, reads above 1L −4.0%, reads above 5L 56 to 47. So the core gain is not just signed cancellation.
- arizona improves on every request metric: MAE/L −11.7%, reads above 5L −22.5%, P99.9/L 6.92 to 6.65.
- Without lbm, training core error still improves slightly (0.0725% to 0.0702%, −3.2%).

Validation (14 anonymized cases) is roughly neutral:
- Core error rises from 0.4504% to 0.4577% (+0.0073 pp, +1.6%). Excluding val7 it rises from 0.0959% to 0.1044% (+0.0085 pp, +8.8%).
- 6 cases get worse, 6 get better and 2 are identical. Summed per-case changes are +0.167 pp of regressions against −0.064 pp of gains, dominated by val5 (+0.12 pp).
- Request MAE/L improves from 0.05758 to 0.05707 (−0.9%), and absolute drift/L falls 2.3%.
- P99.9/L worsens by 3.4% (2.268 to 2.345), mostly from val11. Reads above 5L change by +12 (+0.7%); reads above 1L fall 0.55%.

Across all 28 cases, equally weighted: core error falls from 0.3095% to 0.2871% (−7.2%) and MAE/L from 0.07333 to 0.07169 (−2.2%).

The candidate improves both primary objectives on training, including a large, request-level-confirmed fix for the worst training failure. On validation, request MAE/L and drift improve slightly and the core-error regression is small in absolute terms. This close call favours promotion, although the validation core-error regression (val5 doubling) is a real cost. Both models remain far better than the stage-entry FixedLat reference: training 23.67% core error and 0.5425 MAE/L versus 0.116% and 0.0863; validation 24.90% and 0.5309 versus 0.458% and 0.0571. The candidate also has fewer reads above 5L than FixedLat (4,191 vs 6,445 in training, 1,640 vs 3,100 in validation).

promotion_review.rationale:
No contract violation was demonstrated. The integrity checks are clean: address_mismatch_pairs is 0 in all 28 cases, and no model admission lacks a recorded latency. Oracle-side unpaired admissions are identical to the incumbent's, and matched-read counts change by at most ±0.15% in any case (largest: arizona −122 reads; val4 +363). The fix does not come from lower coverage.

I compared the incumbent source directly. Three behaviours change together: (1) col_slip, which already existed but was off, is turned on; (2) slip_sync is new, and a slipped read now also raises its bank's col_ok/pre_ok and, for row hits, read_horizon; (3) drain_after_reads=3 is new, so a forced drain now waits only for booked read ACTs. All three are general bandwidth and bank-timing rules tied to DDR timings. None depends on workload names, fixed addresses or future requests. Returned predictions are still computed once at admission and never revised; only internal calendar and bank state is updated.

Training (14 cases):
- Core error drops from 0.1685% to 0.1164% (−0.052 pp, −30.9%).
- Request MAE/L drops from 0.08909 to 0.08630 (−3.1%), and mean absolute drift/L from 0.00746 to 0.00436 (−41.6%).
- P99.9/L drops 1.6%. Reads with error above 5L fall from 4,512 to 4,191 (−7.1%); reads above 1L fall 3.6%.
- lbm, the worst training case, supplies about 96% of the core gain: 1.417% to 0.718% (−0.70 pp, −49%).
- Unlike the rejected round 5, lbm's request metrics also improve: MAE/L −2.3%, reads above 1L −4.0%, reads above 5L 56 to 47. So the core gain is not just signed cancellation.
- arizona improves on every request metric: MAE/L −11.7%, reads above 5L −22.5%, P99.9/L 6.92 to 6.65.
- Without lbm, training core error still improves slightly (0.0725% to 0.0702%, −3.2%).

Validation (14 anonymized cases) is roughly neutral:
- Core error rises from 0.4504% to 0.4577% (+0.0073 pp, +1.6%). Excluding val7 it rises from 0.0959% to 0.1044% (+0.0085 pp, +8.8%).
- 6 cases get worse, 6 get better and 2 are identical. Summed per-case changes are +0.167 pp of regressions against −0.064 pp of gains, dominated by val5 (+0.12 pp).
- Request MAE/L improves from 0.05758 to 0.05707 (−0.9%), and absolute drift/L falls 2.3%.
- P99.9/L worsens by 3.4% (2.268 to 2.345), mostly from val11. Reads above 5L change by +12 (+0.7%); reads above 1L fall 0.55%.

Across all 28 cases, equally weighted: core error falls from 0.3095% to 0.2871% (−7.2%) and MAE/L from 0.07333 to 0.07169 (−2.2%).

The candidate improves both primary objectives on training, including a large, request-level-confirmed fix for the worst training failure. On validation, request MAE/L and drift improve slightly and the core-error regression is small in absolute terms. This close call favours promotion, although the validation core-error regression (val5 doubling) is a real cost. Both models remain far better than the stage-entry FixedLat reference: training 23.67% core error and 0.5425 MAE/L versus 0.116% and 0.0863; validation 24.90% and 0.5309 versus 0.458% and 0.0571. The candidate also has fewer reads above 5L than FixedLat (4,191 vs 6,445 in training, 1,640 vs 3,100 in validation).

uncertainty: Three mechanisms change at once (col_slip 0->1, slip_sync 0->1, drain_after_reads 2->3), so their separate contributions are unknown. val5's doubling and val11's tail growth cannot be attributed to a single one.

The training core gain is concentrated in lbm (about 96% of the net). Validation does not confirm a core-error improvement (+1.6%). The lbm gain may be specific to lbm-like write-heavy streaming rather than general.

lbm request error is still very large (MAE/L about 0.50; more than 200k reads above 1L). Its near-zero absolute drift (0.0131 -> 0.0001) partly reflects cancellation between over- and under-predictions, although MAE/L and tail counts also improved.

val7 is still the dominant validation failure (-5.05% core error, underprediction), unchanged in both models (-0.007 pp). It accounts for most of the validation core mean. Its reads above 5L rise from 412 to 439.
Each case is a single deterministic closed-loop ChampSim run. Changes of 0.01 pp or less in core error may reflect closed-loop timing feedback, not model quality.
Unmatched reads (about 9-12% in some cases) are unmeasured for both models, so their errors are unknown.

This is the single-core stage. There is no multicore evidence on how slip_sync and drain_after_reads=3 behave under contention, or whether single-core accuracy will be retained when those rounds begin.
The model is increasingly controller-like, which increases future interpretive risk under the no-internal-scheduler clause. It is not a demonstrated violation.

Coverage changes are negligible (at most about ±40 matched reads per case). lbm's one-read difference between model and oracle admissions comes from the closed-loop simulation, not a matching failure.
Parameter declarations are valid. drain_pending=0.5 is declared with range [0,2]; pending_cap=1 with range [0,1]. All other parameters are identical to the incumbent's.

The source diff is limited to three changes, none adding hidden behaviour. (1) drain_block option 2 and pending_scope are removed; the incumbent never used either (drain_block=1, pending_scope defaulted to 0). (2) The pruning of outstanding reads now runs before the drain. This is equivalent because pending_writebacks already filters on r.done > t. (3) drain_pending is now active.

Predictions are still made once at admission and never revised. The drain_pending mechanism uses only the model's own booked reads (queue-departure and predicted-completion times), a 256-admission running average of the write share, and hardware timing parameters. It changes only the number of writes booked into a forced drain.

No use of future requests, oracle completions, workload names, addresses (beyond same-line forwarding, unchanged from the incumbent) or evaluation identities was found. No internal command scheduler was added; the reservation timeline structure is unchanged.

iteration:7:decision.rationale: I recommend promoting, but it is a close call. No contract violation is shown. Integrity checks are clean in all 28 cases: address_mismatch_pairs=0, model admissions_without_recorded_latency=0, and coverage moves by at most ~40 reads per case. The source differs from the incumbent in three ways. The new drain_pending=0.5 and pending_cap=1 are declared in range. Two options the incumbent never used (drain_block=2, pending_scope) are removed. One cleanup step is moved earlier, which changes no behaviour. The new mechanism uses only the model's own booked reads, a recent average of the write share, and hardware timings. It changes only how many buffered writes a forced drain books at the next read's admission; issued predictions are never revised. On the primary objectives, training improves clearly. Mean training core error falls from 0.1164% to 0.0965% (-0.020 pp, -17.1%). Training request MAE/L falls from 0.08630 to 0.08484 (-1.7%), and 6 of the 7 changed training cases improve MAE/L. The core-error gain comes from lbm, the worst training case: 0.718% to 0.431% (-0.29 pp, -40%). The request level confirms it: lbm MAE/L -1.7% and reads above 1L -1.9%, with coverage unchanged, so this is not cancellation or lost samples. gap_sssp's tail improves materially: 5L count -8.4% and tail metric -9.0%. Validation neither confirms nor contradicts the gain. Core error changes by +0.0002 pp (+0.04%) and MAE/L by +0.08%; only 4 of 14 cases change, and the dominant val7 failure (-5.05%) is untouched. Over all 28 cases weighted equally, core error falls 3.4% and MAE/L falls 1.0%. The cost is a shift in severe tails. Typical errors fall (reads above 1L: training -2.2%, validation -0.1%), but reads above 5L rise in most changed cases. Across training and validation the 5L count is roughly flat (-110 in training, +103 in validation). The physical idea is plausible: fills during a forced drain evict writebacks that lengthen the drain. Unlike the rejected round-5 setting (drain_pending=1), this version improves lbm's request-level accuracy along with its core error. I judge the primary-metric gain to outweigh small, low-frequency tail regressions, but the gain is concentrated in one case and validation does not reproduce it.
uncertainty: The training core-error gain rests on a single case: lbm accounts for essentially all of it, and without lbm training core error is +0.9% worse. The validation core error does not replicate it (+0.04%), so the gain may not generalise beyond write-heavy streaming workloads like lbm.
The value 0.5 was chosen after drain_pending=1 was rejected in round 5. With so few settings tried, part of the lbm gain may come from tuning to lbm rather than from better physics.

Severe errors are redistributed rather than removed. Reads above 1L fall broadly, but reads above 5L rise in 7 of the 10 changed cases, and validation 5L rises 6.3%. The fixed writes-per-read estimate may overestimate drain length in some phases, pushing later reads into extreme overprediction.

The largest remaining validation failure (val7, -5.05% core error) is untouched. Validation mean core error (0.458%) is still dominated by it, so this round leaves the most serious generalisation weakness unaddressed.
Each case is a single run. Several of the per-case core-error differences (about 0.001–0.005 pp) are small enough that they may not be meaningful.

The candidate's own explanation of drain physics (the discount on fills that write back before the drain ends, and the pipeline-depth cap) was treated as unverified. The model reads nothing that would show whether those writebacks actually arrive during the drain. Synthetic and replay diagnostics were not used as decision evidence.

promotion_review.rationale: I recommend promoting, but it is a close call. No contract violation is shown. Integrity checks are clean in all 28 cases: address_mismatch_pairs=0, model admissions_without_recorded_latency=0, and coverage moves by at most ~40 reads per case. The source differs from the incumbent in three ways. The new drain_pending=0.5 and pending_cap=1 are declared in range. Two options the incumbent never used (drain_block=2, pending_scope) are removed. One cleanup step is moved earlier, which changes no behaviour. The new mechanism uses only the model's own booked reads, a recent average of the write share, and hardware timings. It changes only how many buffered writes a forced drain books at the next read's admission; issued predictions are never revised. On the primary objectives, training improves clearly. Mean training core error falls from 0.1164% to 0.0965% (-0.020 pp, -17.1%). Training request MAE/L falls from 0.08630 to 0.08484 (-1.7%), and 6 of the 7 changed training cases improve MAE/L. The core-error gain comes from lbm, the worst training case: 0.718% to 0.431% (-0.29 pp, -40%). The request level confirms it: lbm MAE/L -1.7% and reads above 1L -1.9%, with coverage unchanged, so this is not cancellation or lost samples. gap_sssp's tail improves materially: 5L count -8.4% and tail metric -9.0%. Validation neither confirms nor contradicts the gain. Core error changes by +0.0002 pp (+0.04%) and MAE/L by +0.08%; only 4 of 14 cases change, and the dominant val7 failure (-5.05%) is untouched. Over all 28 cases weighted equally, core error falls 3.4% and MAE/L falls 1.0%. The cost is a shift in severe tails. Typical errors fall (reads above 1L: training -2.2%, validation -0.1%), but reads above 5L rise in most changed cases. Across training and validation the 5L count is roughly flat (-110 in training, +103 in validation). The physical idea is plausible: fills during a forced drain evict writebacks that lengthen the drain. Unlike the rejected round-5 setting (drain_pending=1), this version improves lbm's request-level accuracy along with its core error. I judge the primary-metric gain to outweigh small, low-frequency tail regressions, but the gain is concentrated in one case and validation does not reproduce it.
uncertainty: The training core-error gain rests on a single case: lbm accounts for essentially all of it, and without lbm training core error is +0.9% worse. The validation core error does not replicate it (+0.04%), so the gain may not generalise beyond write-heavy streaming workloads like lbm.
The value 0.5 was chosen after drain_pending=1 was rejected in round 5. With so few settings tried, part of the lbm gain may come from tuning to lbm rather than from better physics.

Severe errors are redistributed rather than removed. Reads above 1L fall broadly, but reads above 5L rise in 7 of the 10 changed cases, and validation 5L rises 6.3%. The fixed writes-per-read estimate may overestimate drain length in some phases, pushing later reads into extreme overprediction.

The largest remaining validation failure (val7, -5.05% core error) is untouched. Validation mean core error (0.458%) is still dominated by it, so this round leaves the most serious generalisation weakness unaddressed.
Each case is a single run. Several of the per-case core-error differences (about 0.001–0.005 pp) are small enough that they may not be meaningful.

The candidate's own explanation of drain physics (the discount on fills that write back before the drain ends, and the pipeline-depth cap) was treated as unverified. The model reads nothing that would show whether those writebacks actually arrive during the drain. Synthetic and replay diagnostics were not used as decision evidence.

contract_findings: Mechanical integrity is clean in all 28 cases (14 training, 14 validation): address_mismatch_pairs=0 and admissions_without_recorded_latency=0.

The candidate and incumbent parameter files are byte-identical: arrival_model=3, arrival_buckets=32, drain_after_reads=3, drain_block=1, same_cycle_writes=1, col_slip=1, slip_sync=1, drain_pending=0.5, pending_cap=1. All values are within their declared ranges.

Active source change: a share_weight bias correction of the write_share running average, used through writes_per_read() in pending_writebacks(). It uses only the types of requests already admitted. It reads no future requests, oracle internals, or workload identity.

The enter_forced() and drain_to_low() extractions reproduce the incumbent's inline forced-entry and drain-to-low-watermark logic. forced_at now sits in a shared helper, but its value is unchanged while drain_anticipate is 0.

The new drain_anticipate option (default 0, not set in parameters.json) is dead code under the frozen configuration. If enabled, it would use only the model's own predicted completion times (in_flight) and the recent write ratio, not future requests. Its own comment says it makes the timeline run slow.
Predictions are still returned once at admission and never revised. There is no per-cycle command scheduler, and there are no workload-, address-, or evaluation-specific branches.
No demonstrated contract violation.
improvements: Training lbm request MAE/L: 0.495397 vs 0.496090 (-0.0007 absolute, -0.14% relative; 128.20 vs 128.38 cycles). This is noise-level and measured on a population 94 reads larger.
Training lbm reads with error over 5L: 44 vs 56 (-12 of about 921k reads). Reads over 1L: 196,018 vs 196,765 (-747, -0.38%).
Training lbm extreme errors are slightly smaller: max +1210 vs +1335 cycles, min -1943 vs -1955 cycles. These are isolated maxima and are not a sufficient basis for promotion.
Training lbm coverage: 921,190 vs 921,096 matched reads (0.99380 vs 0.99370). This is a coverage change, not an accuracy gain.

Physically, dividing a zero-initialized write-share average by its accumulated weight is a principled correction for the writes-per-read estimate early in the run. It has no measurable effect beyond the cold start.
iteration:8:decision.rationale: There is no demonstrated contract violation. The two parameter files are byte-identical. Diffing the sources shows one active behavioral change. The candidate debiases the write-share running average (EWMA) by dividing it by its accumulated weight, share_weight = 1-(255/256)^n. The debiased value reaches the model only through writes_per_read() inside pending_writebacks() (drain_pending=0.5). Its effect fades after roughly the first 1,000 admissions after the cold controller start: the weight is about 0.63 at 256 admissions and about 0.98 at 1,000. The candidate also moves the forced-drain logic into enter_forced()/drain_to_low() without changing behavior, and adds a drain_anticipate option. That option defaults to 0 and is not set, so it is inactive. The measurements match this small scope. All 14 validation cases are byte-identical, so the validation means are unchanged: core 0.45792%, MAE/L 0.057115, P99.9/L 2.3931, tail 0.7569, absolute drift 0.004221. The dominant validation failure (one case at -5.05% core error) is unchanged. Thirteen of 14 training cases are also identical. Only lbm changes, and it moves in both directions at noise level. lbm core error is +0.00076 pp worse (0.43158% vs 0.43082%, +0.18% relative, overprediction in both). MAE/L is 0.14% better (0.495397 vs 0.496090). Reads over 5L fall from 56 to 44 and reads over 1L fall by 747 (-0.38%). But P99.9/L is 0.1% worse, P99 is 603 vs 601, and the tail metric is 0.3% worse (2.3301 vs 2.3224). lbm also matches 94 more reads (921,190 vs 921,096), so the populations differ slightly. The training means change by negligible amounts: core 0.096560% vs 0.096505% (+0.00005 pp, +0.06% relative, worse), MAE/L 0.084792 vs 0.084841 (-0.06%, better), P99.9/L +0.01% worse, tail +0.05% worse, absolute drift 0.004457 vs 0.004468. Against the stage-entry FixedLat reference, both models keep the same gains. On training, core error falls from 23.67% to about 0.097% (about a 99.6% reduction) and MAE/L from 0.5425 to about 0.085 (about 84% lower). On validation, core error falls from 24.90% to 0.458% (about 98.2% lower) and MAE/L from 0.5309 to 0.0571 (about 89% lower). This is a single-core round, so single-core accuracy is fully retained and there is no multicore evidence to weigh. The debiasing is physically sensible, but it is a cold-start refinement with no measurable benefit. Its only visible effect is a mixed perturbation on one training case, well within closed-loop variation, and it adds an untested dormant option. The benefit is unconvincing, so the incumbent is kept.

contract_findings: Mechanical integrity is clean. address_mismatch_pairs = 0 and model admissions_without_recorded_latency = 0 in all 28 cases. Matched-read coverage is equal to or slightly above the incumbent's (e.g. val4 +295, val2 +140, val8 +130, gap_sssp +63; val7 -54, val1 -4). Differences in admission counts are small closed-loop effects, so coverage does not explain any metric change.

The source diff against the incumbent is limited to: the pre_wait parameter (default 0, range 0-4, candidate value 1), its use in plan_open() (PRE = max(earliest, pre_ok + pre_wait)), its member variable, and new comments. parameters.json differs only by the added "pre_wait": 1.

The change reads only DRAM timing parameters and model-internal bank state at admission. It does not look at future requests or oracle internals, does not specialize to workloads, addresses or evaluation identities, and does not revise issued predictions. It adds no per-cycle command selection. No contract violation is demonstrated.

Recurring watch item, not a violation: the reservation timeline keeps getting more controller-like (write-mode replay, slips, and now precharge-timing detail). It still books once at admission and never revises predictions.
improvements: Request MAE/L: training 0.084841 -> 0.083706 (-0.0011, -1.34%); validation 0.057115 -> 0.055087 (-0.0020, -3.55%). iteration:9:decision.rationale: Keep the incumbent. The candidate changes one thing: a new parameter, pre_wait=1 (range 0-4). Planning a bank conflict now uses PRE = max(earliest, pre_ok + pre_wait) instead of max(earliest, pre_ok). Physically, when the precharge has to wait for the bank's own limits (tRAS, tRTP or write recovery), the precharge and the next row activation both happen one cycle later. Combined with rp_adjust=-1, the next activation lands a full tRP after that limit, while a conflict on an idle bank keeps tRP-1. The same code books both reads and writes, so write drains and later bookings shift too. The change is generic, runs only at admission and breaks no rule. The mechanical integrity checks are clean. The decision therefore rests on the evidence, which is mixed and does not clear the bar. Request MAE/L improves broadly but modestly: training 0.084841 -> 0.083706 (-1.34%), validation 0.057115 -> 0.055087 (-3.55%), better in 25 of 28 cases. Core-cycle error, the other primary objective, gets worse in both groups. Training goes 0.096505% -> 0.10883% (+0.0123 pp, +12.8%), or +21.5% excluding lbm. Validation goes 0.457919% -> 0.46140% (+0.0035 pp, +0.76%). The validation total only looks close to even because one case, val3, gains 0.474 pp. Seven other validation cases lose a combined +0.574 pp, including the largest failure, val7, which goes from -5.05% to -5.35% (+0.30 pp). Excluding val3 and val7, validation core error rises 0.0738% -> 0.0924% (+25%). Every regressing case except val7 moves toward overpredicting core cycles. Mean |signed drift|/L also rises on both groups: +1.7% training, +7.2% validation. So the incumbent's better core error does not come from errors cancelling out. The candidate's per-request errors are tighter but shifted upward, and its core error follows that bias. Training severe tails also worsen: reads with error > 5L rise 4,081 -> 4,312 (+5.7%). Earlier reviewers rejected gains carried by a single workload (R5, R8) and warned about drift toward overprediction (R4). A core-error regression on both groups, a worse val7, and a validation gain resting on one case outweigh the 1-4% MAE/L gain. Against the stage-entry FixedLat, both models remain far better: the candidate is at 0.109% vs 23.669% core error and 0.0837 vs 0.5425 MAE/L on training, and 0.461% vs 24.903% and 0.0551 vs 0.5309 on validation. That is not what separates them.
